Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

sasonr 0.0.0.9000

sasonr is in early development and not on CRAN yet. This section lists what the development version provides.

Running SAS programs

  • PROC FORMAT PICTURE: digit selectors (0 suppresses leading zeros, 1-9 keep them), the default multiplier from the decimals of the picture, MULT=, PREFIX= (also for a range of negative values), message characters, NOEDIT, ranges with OTHER=[format]; values longer than the selectors keep their last digits. FILL=, ROUND and DATATYPE= fail loud.

  • PROC PRINT narrows the gap between columns (to 3, 2 or 1) to fit a table on the line; a table that does not fit with a gap of 1 (column panels) still fails loud. The NOTEs about data sets created and read wrap at the line size.

  • A small PAGESIZE= that would page the log fails loud (the log’s page headers are not implemented).

  • The listing starts at NOCENTER: printed output read in the R console is left-aligned, without the blank margin of centred output (the HTML output stays centred). OPTIONS CENTER; in the program centres both, OPTIONS NOCENTER; neither; options(sasonr.center = TRUE) starts sessions at CENTER.

  • ODS TRACE ON; / ODS TRACE OFF;: the “Output Added” lines of the PROC MEANS Summary and PROC PRINT tables (other tables fail loud).

  • PUT of array elements (put a[2]= writes the element’s name, a[i], a[*] the values of all elements) and PUT _ALL_; (every variable as name=value, then _ERROR_ and _N_). PUT _CHARACTER_/_NUMERIC_ and PUT; fail loud.

  • UPDATE master transaction; with BY: per BY group the first master observation with the transactions applied in order (missing values do not replace values, the special missing values .A-.Z do; UPDATEMODE= NOMISSINGCHECK replaces with missing values too), the group’s other master observations unchanged, new BY groups from the transactions. UPDATE without BY, with IN= and ._ in a transaction fail loud.

  • SET with POINT=: direct access by observation number (also over several data sets); an invalid number sets _ERROR_ and leaves the PDV; the POINT= variable starts at 0 and is not written to output data sets; no observations-read NOTE. A step whose only readers use POINT= and that has no STOP statement, POINT= with BY or with data set options that select observations fail loud.

  • Multi-dimensional arrays (array m[2,3], bounds per dimension), with DIM/LBOUND/HBOUND of a dimension (DIM2(m), DIM(m, 2)); DO OVER of an implicitly subscripted array (array v v1-v4;, index _I_); a sum statement on an array element with a constant subscript (or of a TEMPORARY array).

  • Read-only libraries: LIBNAME ref XPORT 'file'; reads the member of a transport file (version 5) in SET, MERGE, PROC DATA= and data set options, with the attributes of its variables (lengths, formats, informats, labels) and special missing values; LIBNAME ref CLEAR;. Members are read when a step names them (ref.member) and are not part of WORK. A directory library (LIBNAME ref 'dir';) is assigned, but reading a .sas7bdat member, writing to a library, other engines and options and a transport file with several members fail loud.

  • Implicit conversions in the DATA step: a character variable or a quoted string in arithmetic, MIN/MAX, AND/OR or compared with a number is read as a number (invalid data: missing, _ERROR_ and the “Invalid numeric data” NOTE); a number assigned to a character variable is written with BEST12. (its rightmost characters for a shorter variable); the conversion NOTEs list the places, after the NOTEs of the compilation phase. Other operands (function results, expressions) fail loud.

  • ODS HTML FILE="path" <STYLE=HTMLBlue>; writes the HTML document of the procedure output up to ODS HTML CLOSE; to that file (other ODS HTML options, a directory that does not exist and a destination left open fail loud).

  • %SYSFUNC(GETOPTION(ENCODING)) returns the session encoding, UTF-8; other options of GETOPTION fail loud.

  • sas_script() of a program with %INCLUDE runs the included steps once (the statement itself is no longer replayed).

  • MERGE without BY (one-to-one): the n-th observation of each data set; the variables of a data set whose observations are all read are missing.

  • A character variable read by SET or MERGE takes the length it has in the step (a LENGTH statement before the SET or MERGE), padded or truncated (it kept the data set’s length before).

  • DATA step hash objects: DECLARE HASH (also DCL) with dataset:, ordered: and hashexp:, the methods DEFINEKEY, DEFINEDATA, DEFINEDONE, ADD, FIND, CHECK, REPLACE and REMOVE (also with key: and data: arguments) and the NUM_ITEMS attribute, in the value of an assignment, in an IF condition or as a statement. FIND copies the data variables into the PDV; a key that is not there returns 160038, ADD of a key that is there 160036, REMOVE of a key that is not there 160032; REPLACE of a key that is not there adds it. OUTPUT(DATASET:) of an object with ordered: 'a' or 'd' writes its data variables in key order (the keys without DEFINEDATA; definedata(all: 'yes') with DATASET:). A DECLARE that runs again makes a new, empty object. DECLARE HITER over an ordered object: FIRST, LAST, NEXT and PREV copy the data variables of the entry; NEXT before FIRST starts at the first entry, past the last one the call returns 160038 and the next NEXT starts over. OUTPUT or an iterator without ORDERED:, SUMINC:, a failing method call statement and a method call in an expression that also reads variables fail loud.

  • The row-by-row (L3) code of a DATA step shows the step’s statements: the per-step state (the PDV prototype, reset values, OUTPUT buffers, error dump) is one object made by sas_step_state(), each SET or MERGE statement reads with pdv <- sas_set_next(.r, pdv) or sas_merge_next(), an iteration runs in sas_iter_run({ ... }) and ends with if (sas_iter_done(.st, .status)) break. DO loops with constant bounds are while loops, DO UNTIL without CONTINUE tests after the body, an empty OTHERWISE writes no empty else, and _ERROR_ is synced once per iteration when the step neither reads it nor writes lines of its own.

  • Each SET and MERGE statement of a DATA step reads with its own reader: several SET statements (the step stops at the first end of file), SET or MERGE in an IF branch, if 0 then set ds; (the variables without a read) and DOW loops (do until (last.id); set ds; by id; ... end;, also DO WHILE). A BY statement belongs to the SET or MERGE statement before it, also inside a DO loop; FIRST. and LAST. variables start at 1, END= and IN= variables at 0. A SET with BY reads one observation ahead, which the observations-read NOTE counts; a SET that never ran writes no such NOTE. BY statements in IF or SELECT blocks, BY statements with different variables in one step, several MERGE statements and a WHERE statement with several readers fail loud.

  • The line a macro generates is echoed under its NOTE without the leading blanks of the macro text, also when the macro generates a whole step.

  • INPUT: invalid data on a line of a record that the error lines do not show adds the two NOTEs about errors outside the printed range.

  • The R code of sas_translate() and sas_script() (also the tidy form) is laid out like the air formatter writes it: an expression that fits in 80 columns stays on one line; a longer call puts one argument per line, a pipeline one step per line; a mutate() of several columns writes one column per line. The code that runs is the code shown.

  • PROC UNIVARIATE writes its printed output (without NOPRINT): the Moments, Basic Statistical Measures, Tests for Location, Quantiles and Extreme Observations tables of each analysis variable, with the mode Note and the Missing Values table (special missing values included), the label of a variable after its name, also under OPTIONS CENTER. BY, CLASS, WEIGHT and OUTPUT with printed output, VARDEF= and PCTLDEF=, a quantile column that needs the E form, skewness or kurtosis whose last digits depend on the order of the sums fail loud.

  • A session now starts at OPTIONS CENTER, the SAS default (it started at NOCENTER): each title line, procedure title and table heading is centred on its own, each table as a whole, and BY lines are written between dashes. This covers PROC PRINT (with its N line), PROC MEANS, PROC FREQ with its statistics tables, PROC TABULATE, PROC CONTENTS (also the CONTENTS statement of PROC DATASETS) and PROC SQL. The option sasonr.center = FALSE (or the environment variable SASONR_CENTER=FALSE) starts sessions at NOCENTER. sas_html() centres the titles and the tables under CENTER and writes them on the left under NOCENTER (it used to centre the titles only).

  • PROC PRINT column positions: a formatted number’s field is the format width and its heading is right-aligned; an unformatted number (and Obs) is centred rounding up, a character column rounding down; an unformatted column whose values are rounded to two decimals because of their magnitude is laid out like a formatted one; the heading of a character column whose values are of uneven widths starts in the first position (columns up to 16 wide; wider ones fail loud); a number under a user-defined format is laid out as text; character values are written without their leading blanks; a formatted number keeps the blanks its format writes after it (PERCENT.); a missing value of an unformatted number sits in the decimal point column; headings of several lines follow the same rules. Before, headings and fields could sit a position or more to the left or right of their place.

  • PROC FREQ: in a crosstabulation the column variable heading starts at least five blanks after the row variable heading; the values of a number under a user-defined format are left-aligned in a one-way table (the heading stays right-aligned); the “Frequency Missing” line is centred under the table rounding up.

  • PROC CONTENTS: the Len column widens for lengths of more than three digits; a variable table wider than LINESIZE (long labels) fails loud.

  • PROC SQL: a column label with blanks wraps word by word at the width of the column or of its longest word (it was cut in two lines only); a report wider than LINESIZE fails loud (it was written wider than the line, where the columns are narrowed).

  • PROC MEANS: the “Analysis Variable” heading is centred over its table (it started in the first position).

  • PROC FREQ statistics tables are laid out column for column: the CMH summary, the common odds ratio and relative risks, the Breslow-Day test, the risk estimates, the odds ratio and relative risks, the confidence limits of RELRISK / RISKDIFF CL= and the exact chi-square tests had their columns separated by single blanks; their headings, the “Chi-Square Test” heading of a one-way table and the binomial headings are centred over their tables, and the “Test” heading of TESTP= / TESTF= sits over its column.

  • PROC CONTENTS: the headings “Variables in Creation Order”, “Alphabetic List of Variables and Attributes” and “Sort Information” are centred over their table (they started in the first position).

  • PROC CONTENTS SHORT no longer writes the data set attributes (only the list of variables).

  • PROC CONTENTS: the second column of the data set attributes is 57 characters wide (it was 56, so the third column started one position early).

  • PROC PRINT headings from variable names: a name without a lowercase-uppercase change whose piece is still longer than the column splits again at an underscore (abcd_efgh_ijkl on three lines; it was written on two). A name with one lowercase-uppercase change splits there only when it is longer than its values and than 4 characters (AbCd was split); a name with several such changes that is wider than its values now fails loud (it was split at one place).

  • ODS RTF: a PROC PRINT table wider than the page is split into column groups, each a table of its own; the groups are balanced (each takes columns up to the average of the page width and the table width per group), and a column is at most half the page wide. The Obs column or a single ID variable starts every group, each group ends with its own N line, and each BY group is split on its own. A split table with several ID variables or sum rows still fails loud.

  • An ARRAY of existing character variables now keeps the length a LENGTH statement gave them: storing through an element reference (c{j} = ...) no longer cuts the value to 8 characters. An array of character variables of different lengths fails loud.

  • The Dw.p format: the value is rounded to a number of decimals that depends on the width, p (3 when omitted), the sign and the magnitude of the value, so that values of one magnitude line up on the decimal point. Widths 6 to 14 and p = 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6 are supported (a value that needs the E form is written as BESTw. writes it); other widths and p values fail loud. Until the format registry lists it, the format runs with options(sasonr.strict = FALSE) only.

  • PROC PRINT LABEL: a label of three to five words that is wider than the column is written on at most three lines, at the narrowest width that allows it (a longer label still fails loud). A variable name with an underscore and a lowercase-uppercase change that is wider than its values (such as an AUTONAME name) fails loud: SAS splits it, at places not yet measured.

  • PROC SQL reads DICTIONARY.COLUMNS and DICTIONARY.TABLES (and the views SASHELP.VCOLUMN / SASHELP.VTABLE) for the WORK members, data sets and views: a query must restrict libname = 'WORK', and the TABLES columns that depend on the host (dates, sizes, pages, encoding …) fail loud. Other DICTIONARY tables fail loud.

  • The LABEL= data set option on a DATA step output data set sets its label (PROC CONTENTS, DICTIONARY.TABLES).

  • PROC PRINT of a table wider than LINESIZE fails loud (sasonr wrote the lines longer than LINESIZE; SAS stacks the headings or splits the columns).

  • A word or a number that starts no statement in open code (foo;, 1;), and an unresolved macro call at the start of an open-code statement that ends with ; (%nosuch;, %nosuch(1, 2);, with its WARNING), write ERROR 180-322 and start syntax-check mode at the next DATA step (none under NOSYNTAXCHECK); the program may also end there. They failed loud.

  • PROC UNIVARIATE: NOPRINT with OUTPUT OUT= for one or several analysis variables, with BY and one CLASS variable, VARDEF=, PCTLDEF=, PCTLPTS= with PCTLPRE= and PCTLNAME=, and 34 statistics (N NMISS NOBS MEAN SUM STD VAR SKEWNESS KURTOSIS SUMWGT MAX MIN RANGE the quartiles and P1-P99 QRANGE MODE CSS USS CV STDMEAN T PROBT MSIGN PROBM SIGNRANK PROBS). The OUT= columns follow the measured order (by statistic, then variable), carry SAS’s labels, and the data set has type OUT and the label “Selected Summary Statistics” (with the percentile definition when a percentile is requested); the step writes no observations-read NOTE. WEIGHT gives the weighted N, SUM, MEAN, VAR, STD, CSS and USS (other statistics with WEIGHT fail loud). Printed output, FREQ, ID, PCTLPTS= with TO / BY or WEIGHT, the robust and normality statistics, and a signed rank test of more than 20 nonzero differences fail loud.

  • PROC FREQ: a TABLES OUT= data set has the label “Frequency Counts and Percentages”.

  • PROC TABULATE: numbered variable lists (v1-v30) in the VAR and CLASS statements, and as the whole content of parentheses in a TABLE dimension ((v1-v30)*sum); other variable list forms still fail loud. A table without a row dimension that is wider than the line is split into panels in the listing, as one with a row dimension.

  • PROC FREQ crosstable headings: a row variable heading longer than the row label column stays on one line with the column heading (five blanks between them) when both fit the table width, else the column heading goes to the next line; a row value longer than 16 characters is written in pieces of 16 on the statistic lines (sasonr put the column heading on the next line and widened the column).

  • PROC SQL CREATE TABLE records sort information that PROC CONTENTS shows: ORDER BY of result columns (by name, alias or position, with DESC), GROUP BY of one result column and SELECT DISTINCT of one column (with the sort option NODUPKEY when the rows are unique by it), and UNION of one column ordered by it. Query shapes whose sort information is not measured make PROC CONTENTS of the table fail loud. PROC CONTENTS also writes Character Set ASCII (it wrote ANSI), the Sort Option NODUPKEY line, and the names after DESCENDING as stored.

  • PROC FREQ: RELRISK(CL=) together with RISKDIFF(CL=) on a 2x2 table (CL= alone in both) writes both confidence-limit tables, in the listing and in ODS HTML.

  • The WHERE line of the “observations read” NOTE longer than LINESIZE breaks before the word that does not fit, every line but the last at most LINESIZE - 1 columns, continuation lines indented by 6, a word too long for a line cut at LINESIZE - 6 (sasonr wrote it on one line). A PUT of one value wider than LINESIZE writes it cut every LINESIZE characters; a wider value after other items fails loud.

  • sas_script(): a step on whose lines the macro processor wrote a WARNING (an unresolved &name) is kept as SAS text in the trace, so running the script writes the WARNING again.

  • CALL EXECUTE in a DATA step: the text is queued and runs after the step, with “NOTE: CALL EXECUTE generated line.” and the N + text echo of each generated step. Text made of DATA and PROC steps that end with RUN; or QUIT; is supported. Macro code in the argument runs at the call (%LET, %PUT between the step’s PUT lines, macro calls); the text it generates is queued, and macro code that generates none writes “NOTE: CALL EXECUTE routine executed successfully, but no SAS statements were generated.”. An entry without text keeps its number. A macro call kept by %NRSTR runs when its entry runs (one echo line for the entry). An echo longer than LINESIZE breaks at the blank before the word that does not fit, the lines after it starting in column 1; a word longer than LINESIZE starts a new line and is cut. Other macro quoting, a numeric argument, an ERROR in an entry with more than one step fail loud; an ERROR in a one-step entry stops that step and the queue goes on. sas_translate() keeps such a program as SAS text from the step with CALL EXECUTE on.

  • options(sasonr.start_time = <POSIXct>) sets the session start time that the automatic macro variables SYSDATE, SYSDATE9, SYSDAY and SYSTIME report, so a program that branches on &SYSDAY gives the same result on any day.

  • A DATA step whose statement is ignored after a syntax ERROR (ERROR 76-322, e.g. PUT() without a format: ERROR 388-185) compiles on: the ignored assignment leaves its target numeric, the type conversion NOTE of the later statements is written, and a later character format on a numeric variable writes its WARNING and ERROR 48-59 at its own line. In PUT, a character format on a numeric variable writes the WARNING; $w. writes the value with w., $QUOTE. and $CHAR. stop the step with ERROR 48-59.

  • $QUOTEw. with a width too small for the text cuts it at the width: a doubled quote that the cut would split is dropped, and $QUOTE1. writes a blank (an Unsupported error before).

  • ODS RTF FILE="path"; and ODS RTF CLOSE; write the RTF document of the PROC PRINT and PROC TABULATE tables (default style) when the destination closes. PROC TABULATE: merged row titles and headings, class heading rows anywhere in the row dimension, the page text of a page dimension (one section per page), the same width rule as PROC PRINT, a column heading over several columns setting a minimum width for each of them. A table wider than 9322 twips (it may be split into column groups) and characters whose advance is not measured are an Unsupported error. PROC PRINT: the table rows, borders, heading and row-header styles, BY lines, SPLIT= line breaks and the column widths (from the measured character advances of the default fonts); the N line sets a minimum width for each column it spans (also with BY). Other procedures, options of the ODS RTF statement, titles in the document, and a destination left open at the end of the program are an Unsupported error.

  • PROC PRINT supports OBS=, N, LABEL, SPLIT= and the ID, BY, SUM and SUMBY statements: one page per BY group with its byline, observation numbers that continue across pages, subtotals per BY group and the grand total. Each value field is as wide as its widest entry and centred under the heading. Several BY variables with SUM, SUMBY other than the BY variable, N together with SUM, a label of more than two words without SPLIT=, an ID variable that is also a BY variable, BY on unsorted data, VAR options and DOUBLE are an Unsupported error (DOUBLE was accepted and ignored before).

  • The ODS table class is now sasonr_ods_table, like the other classes of the package.

  • PROC TABULATE supports the BY statement (each BY group on its own page under the titles and its BY line, percentages per group, #BYVAL(var) in a title) and the percentages COLPCTN, ROWPCTN, REPPCTN, PAGEPCTN, COLPCTSUM, ROWPCTSUM and PCTN<var> / PCTSUM<var> with class variables as the denominator. A table of several panels can now have a page dimension.

  • PROC TABULATE CLASSDATA= (with or without EXCLUSIVE), the CLASS option PRELOADFMT with the TABLE option PRINTMISS, and PRINTMISS when every combination of levels occurs: the levels of the CLASSDATA= data set and of the format ranges join the levels of the data in internal order; a level without observations has N 0. These options with more than one CLASS variable, with BY or OUT=, with ORDER=, DESCENDING or MISSING, or with a format range that is not one value are an Unsupported error.

  • PROC TABULATE OUT= writes the same data set as ODS OUTPUT Table= (one column builder for both); OUT= with BY, with data set options or with an ODS OUTPUT request in the same step is an Unsupported error.

  • PROC TABULATE ORDER=FREQ puts tied levels in data order (the order of their first observation); ties under ORDER=FREQ with DESCENDING are an Unsupported error.

  • sas_means_df(), sas_tabulate_df() and sas_transpose_df() run one procedure on a data frame without a program and return its ODS table (or the output data set of PROC TRANSPOSE). They call the computation that sas_run() calls for the same step, with the specification from the same parser and builder, so the values are the same. sas_log() and sas_html() are S3 generics with methods for these results; as.data.frame() drops the table attributes.

  • %SYSFUNC accepts BAND, BYTE, CONSTANT, COUNT, COUNTW, PUTC, RANK, REPEAT, REVERSE, and the clock functions DATETIME, TIME and TODAY, now supported in the macro context (function registry); DATETIME and TIME are zero-argument calls there like TODAY.

  • PROC FREQ BINOMIAL(EXACT) gives the exact (Clopper-Pearson) confidence limits, as CL=EXACT; before, it ran the exact binomial test (which is the EXACT BINOMIAL statement) and kept the Wald limits. BINOMIAL(CORRECT) applies the continuity correction to the Wald limits and to the test also without CL= (before, it was ignored there), with the footnote of the listing.

  • PROC FREQ CHISQ together with BINOMIAL for a one-way table writes the chi-square test, then the binomial block, then the sample size once, whatever the order of the options; before, the chi-square test was left out.

  • PROC FREQ TABLES / NOPRINT suppresses only the frequency and crosstabulation tables: the statistics requested (CHISQ, FISHER, the multiway CMH summary, BINOMIAL) are written; before, the request wrote nothing. A step whose requests are all NOPRINT without statistics or OUT= writes the NOTE that processing terminates and reads no data.

  • PROC FREQ runs on the same PROC pipeline: its one-way and two-way tables are ODS tables (OneWayFreqs, CrossTabFreqs with one row per cell and per total, in $ods), so are the CHISQ and FISHER results of a two-way table (ChiSq, FishersExact), RELRISK (RelativeRisks, RelRiskCL), RISKDIFF (RiskDiffCol1, RiskDiffCol2, PdiffCLs), BINOMIAL (Binomial, BinomialCLs, BinomialTest), the one-way chi-square test (OneWayChiSq), NLEVELS (NLevels) and the multiway CMH summary (CMH, CommonRelRisks, BreslowDayTest), and sas_freq_df() returns them for a data frame. The stratum crosstabulations of a multiway request and the LIST table are ODS tables too (CrossTabFreqs, List).

  • sas_html() draws the PROC FREQ one-way tables, crosstabulations (with the cell-statistics legend), the chi-square table, Fisher’s exact test (2x2), the column risk estimates of RISKDIFF, the odds ratio and relative risks of RELRISK, the confidence limits of RELRISK(CL=) and RISKDIFF(CL=), the BINOMIAL tables, the one-way chi-square test, NLEVELS, the stratum crosstabulations of a multiway request and the statistics of each stratum, the LIST table and the multiway CMH summary, as in the HTML destination. It is an Unsupported error, naming the procedure and its SAS line, when the HTML destination received output that has no HTML view yet (PROC PRINT, the other PROC FREQ tables, n-way and LIST tables); before, that output was left out of the document.

  • The trace of a run (sas_script() of a sas_run() result) keeps what a macro invocation writes with %PUT outside its steps, with the new verb sas_macro_put(); before, those lines were missing from the script’s log.

  • The PROC verbs take line as one line per statement (the PROC statement first), and sas_script() passes it when statements share a line, so the messages that name a line inside the step name the program’s line.

  • A translation without a run (sas_translate(), sas_script()) applies the KEEP=, DROP= and RENAME= options of a PROC MEANS OUTPUT data set to the variables it gives the following steps; before, a later step could select _TYPE_ and _FREQ_ that KEEP= had removed.

  • The lang of a sas_script() DATA step node runs a step whose vectorised code falls back to row-by-row execution; before, it failed with “bad value” (the generated function call lacked its srcref element).

  • sas_proc_print() and sas_proc_tabulate() are step verbs too, and sas_script() writes PROC PRINT and PROC TABULATE steps with them.

  • sas_proc_freq() and sas_proc_transpose() are step verbs like sas_proc_sort() and sas_proc_means(): they take a session, the options of the PROC statement and one argument per statement, and sas_script() writes PROC FREQ and PROC TRANSPOSE steps with them. The run-time helpers that had these names until now are internal.

  • ODS OUTPUT Table= (or the path Tabulate.Report.Table=) before a PROC TABULATE step writes the table as a data set: the CLASS variables, then _TYPE_, _PAGE_ and _TABLE_, then one column per analysis variable and statistic (v_N, v_Mean, v_Sum, v_PctN_00_v; N without an analysis variable), one observation per class-level combination. N, MEAN, SUM and PCTN with one TABLE statement are supported; other statistics, F=, labels in the TABLE statement, KEYLABEL, a LABEL statement, CLASS options and an ODS OUTPUT statement inside the step are an Unsupported error.

  • PROC TABULATE tables reach the HTML document of sas_html() while the HTML destination is open: heading rows and the corner cell in <thead>, row titles spanning their sub-rows, N and NMISS without decimals, one table per page of the page dimension under its page text. A heading or MISSTEXT longer than its column, a BOX= text in the corner and F= on an N or NMISS cell are an Unsupported error of sas_html(); the listing is still written.

  • PROC TABULATE prints its tables to the listing: one, two and three dimensions with crossing, concatenation, ALL, labels, F=, BOX= and MISSTEXT=, the row-title area of LINESIZE/4, wrapped headings, column panels with (Continued) and one table per page of the page dimension. The table objects are kept in the result’s ods list. CLASS / MISSING applies to the variables of its own CLASS statement. Layouts outside these rules (and, in strict mode, the statistics not yet in the PROC statistics registry) are an Unsupported error.

  • In-stream data start on the line after the DATALINES (CARDS, LINES, DATALINES4, …) statement. Blanks and /* */ comments may follow the statement on its line; any other text there is now an Unsupported error. Before, that text and the rest of the program were taken as data and the steps after it were silently skipped.

  • Readability passes for the code of vectorised DATA steps (option sasonr.passes, see ?sas_translate): a retained numeric variable set only at FIRST. of a BY group from a column is written as one grouped value per BY group (group_by(), dplyr::first(), ungroup()) instead of the carry-forward helper, and FIRST./LAST. columns that nothing reads are no longer created. sas_run() and sas_script() use the same code; with options(sasonr.passes = character()) the code is unchanged.

  • The level, on_error and scope arguments of sas_run(), sas_translate() and sas_macro_vars() take their exact values only (rlang::arg_match()); an abbreviation such as level = "L" is an error.

  • Internals: the code generator builds its R calls with rlang (call2(), expr(), sym(), exec()), package-held numbers and lists go through vctrs (vec_cast(), list_unchop(), vec_rbind()), and row-wise function calls use purrr, a new dependency.

  • sas_run() runs a SAS program given as text and returns the log, the listing and the WORK data sets; sas_translate() shows the R code that is generated for each step. sas_lex(), sas_parse(), sas_parse_expr() and sas_analyze() expose the lexer, the parser and the static analysis.

  • sas_script() writes the translation of a program (sas_translate()) or the trace of a run (sas_run()) as an R script: one step verb per SAS step (sas_data_step() with the generated code of the step, sas_proc_sort() and sas_proc_means() with the options the program gave, sas_proc_sql(), sas_proc(), sas_options(), sas_title(), sas_global()), each running its step in a session; macro code whose result is known only at run time is kept as SAS text in sas_deferred(). tidy = TRUE writes vectorised DATA steps as dplyr pipes on R variables (with library(tidylog); see sasonr_tidy_log()) and keeps a session only for the other steps. sas_work(trim = FALSE) and sas_session_add() move data sets between R and a session. The internal PROC MEANS helper is now sas_rt_proc_means().

  • sas_check() lists every unsupported feature of a program before anything runs (step, line, feature), where sas_run() stops at the first one. A step that uses a macro variable set only at run time (CALL SYMPUT, INTO :) is reported as checked when the program runs.

  • sas_session() creates a persistent session. Successive sas_run(code, session = s) calls are submissions to that session: WORK data sets, macro variables and macro definitions, user formats, OPTIONS, titles and filerefs carry over. sas_work(), sas_meta(), sas_macro_vars(), sas_log() and sas_listing() read a session; sas_session_close() closes its PROC SQL connection. A submission to a session that is already running one is refused. The Architecture article lists the state that does not carry over between submissions (syntax-check mode, PRXPARSE numbering, log line numbers, PROC SQL left open).

  • There is no default session: function-layer calls outside sas_run() keep no hidden state. PRXPARSE ids need session = (sas_f_prxparse(re, session = s)); pattern texts work without one.

  • sas_export_work() writes the WORK data sets of a result as CSV files together with a table of variable attributes.

  • The exports are explicit: the user API plus the run-time helpers that translated code calls (documented as internal). sas_format() and sas_fmt_best() are internal; use sas_f_putn() and sas_f_putc(), which take the format as text and check it. The PROC SQL helpers sas_f_cvt_*() and sas_f_sql*() are internal exports as well, and sas_titles_once() and sas_untranslated() are new internal exports.

  • Translated code calls only base R, package-prefixed functions and the exported helpers. The code of PROC SQL and PROC DATASETS steps, which sasonr runs itself, is a call of sas_untranslated() that stops with sasonr_unsupported; the sas_translate() page describes the environment in which the code of a step is evaluated.

  • SASHELP members are read from the directory given by options(sasonr.sashelp_dir) or the environment variable SASONR_SASHELP_DIR (<member>.sas7bdat with its column attributes in <member>_meta.csv, or a built .rds). sasonr ships no SASHELP members; without a directory every SASHELP member is missing and fails loud.

The log

  • $log of a result shows the program lines with their numbers (long lines continued on ! lines at LINESIZE), each step’s messages after its lines, compile-time ERRORs after their line with an underscore marker and the error number. OPTIONS SOURCE and NOSOURCE turn the echo on and off.
  • $log of a result and sas_log() now carry the source echo (before: the messages and PUT output only, which sas_log(x, echo = FALSE) gives). The first argument of sas_log() is now x (a result or a session); sas_log(session = s) still works.
  • sas_log(x, format = c("plain", "ansi", "html"), echo = TRUE) gives the log of a result or a session as plain text, as text coloured for the terminal (ERROR red, WARNING green, NOTE blue, with a summary line), or as HTML with CSS classes (sas-note, sas-warning, sas-error, sas-put, sas-src; style sheet in system.file("css", "sasonr.css", package = "sasonr")). echo = FALSE gives the messages and PUT output only.
  • print() of a result shows the coloured view in a terminal with colours; options(sasonr.log_style = "plain") turns it off.
  • $log_events of a result is a tibble of the log events (kind, message id, step, place, text, program line) behind every view.
  • A numeric variable as an operand of || in a DATA step now gives the NOTE “Numeric values have been converted to character values” with the place of the variable. A numeric constant or expression as an operand of || fails loud (unsupported).
  • A DATA step with a SET, MERGE or INPUT statement now stops at the first iteration that ends without executing one, whatever the condition that skipped the read: that iteration completes (its OUTPUT statements run, and DELETE or a subsetting IF drops its observation), then the log shows “NOTE: DATA STEP stopped due to looping.” (before the observations-read NOTEs). A STOP statement in that iteration ends the step without the NOTE. A reading statement in a DO loop or a SELECT group, or a RETURN statement in the step, fails loud when such an iteration happens.

Errors and fail-loud behaviour

  • Features that sasonr does not support raise a condition of class sasonr_unsupported with the SAS line instead of being approximated.
  • Error model: sas_run(on_error = c("sas", "abort")), default "sas" (option sasonr.on_error). After an ERROR in the program the step is not run and syntax-check mode (OBS=0), the documented behaviour of batch jobs, applies to the rest of the program: DATA steps create empty data sets, global statements and macro code still run, PROC SQL errors set NOEXEC for that PROC SQL only, and SYSERR and SYSCC are set. The result has status = "error", errors and error_line. sasonr_unsupported always aborts. Calls of names that are not SAS functions give ERROR 68-185; unknown SET options are syntax errors.
  • In syntax-check mode the TITLE statements of a PROC step and the OPTIONS statements of PROC DATASETS are executed; PROC CONTENTS runs (listing, OUT= with 0 observations); PROC SORT OUT=, PROC FREQ TABLES OUT= and PROC APPEND create a new output data set with 0 observations and 0 variables and keep an existing one; PROC MEANS stops with SYSERR 1012; PROC SQL writes the NOEXEC NOTEs, sets SQLOBS and SQLRC to 0 and ends with SYSERR 1012; the other steps set SYSERR to 3; a DATA step does not replace an existing data set. PROC TRANSPOSE with DATA=, a new OUT= data set and a VAR statement runs on its input with 0 observations. Other forms of PROC TRANSPOSE, PROC FORMAT, PROC SUMMARY and other combinations fail loud.
  • An ERROR in a global statement is not handled like a step ERROR: for LINESIZE= set to a name other than MAX outside a step, sasonr writes ERROR 18-12, sets SYSCC to 1012 and enters syntax-check mode at the next DATA step unless OPTIONS NOSYNTAXCHECK comes first. Other ERRORs in global statements fail loud.
  • The empty data sets left by a failing step are derived from the parsed step (types, lengths, LENGTH, RETAIN, ARRAY); when they cannot be derived, sasonr fails loud.
  • Strict mode (options(sasonr.strict = TRUE), the default): a program that uses a function, format, informat or procedure statistic whose status is approximate (the last bits of numeric results may not be exact) or unsupported, or a function in a context in which it is not supported (DATA step, WHERE, PROC SQL, %SYSFUNC), stops with a condition of class sasonr_strict_error (a subclass of sasonr_unsupported). With options(sasonr.strict = FALSE) such features run: the log of the submission ends with one NOTE that lists the approximate features used, and each feature signals one warning of class sasonr_strict_warning per submission. Arguments outside the domain in which a function’s results are exact go through the same gate. PUTN, PUTC, INPUTN and INPUTC check the format they name at run time. See ?sasonr_strict.
  • Feature statuses (supported, partial, approximate, unsupported, not_comparable) are available through sas_feature_registry() and sas_proc_stat_registry().
  • sasonr targets SAS 9.4 and has one behaviour.

DATA step

  • A numeric arithmetic expression as an operand of || is converted to character text, the conversion NOTE giving the place of its operator (a prefix -, + or NOT at that operator). The places of one line are listed in column order. A constant, function call or comparison operand still fails loud.

  • Lengths and other integer tokens: ATTRIB LENGTH= no longer reads $8.5 as 85 (a fractional length is truncated, $8.5 is 8); a numeric length is range-checked on the value as written (8.5 is an error, 3.5 is 3), also in LENGTH. A fractional ARRAY dimension or initial-value repetition, INPUT end column, INPUT #n pointer and FILE LRECL= is a syntax error. A PUT item wider than the FILE LRECL fails loud.

  • VLENGTH() of a numeric variable returns its declared length (3 to 8).

  • Hand-written lexer (strings, comments, name, date and hex literals, special missing values, DATALINES blocks, macro tokens), recursive-descent statement parser and Pratt expression parser with the SAS operator precedence. The AST keeps the program as written.

  • DATA steps are compiled to R code at three levels: vectorised dplyr code (L1), grouped vectorised code for recognised patterns such as BY groups with FIRST./LAST., RETAIN accumulators, baseline carry-forward and unconditional LAG (L2), and an explicit row loop that follows the DATA step execution rules otherwise (L3). A vectorised step that needs row-by-row diagnostics is re-run row by row.

  • _ERROR_ and the data error diagnostics (PDV dump in the log), SAS-style log NOTEs for missing values and mathematical operations, and the variable attribute model (length, format, informat, label, name case).

  • INPUT statement pointers and modifiers, INFILE options, the FILE statement and LINESIZE.

  • The declarative statements of a DATA step (WHERE, KEEP, DROP, RENAME, BY, the attribute statements and the output list) are collected into slots of an intermediate representation, and the executable statements are lowered to a control-flow graph. Data-flow facts on that graph decide the step level. The generated R code is built as R calls and evaluated directly; sas_translate() shows the deparsed text.

  • Data set options (KEEP=, DROP=, RENAME=, WHERE=, IN=, FIRSTOBS=, OBS=) of DATA step input and output data sets, PROC DATA=, PROC OUT= and PROC SQL tables go through one component. An invalid option on an input data set is an ERROR and stops the step; an unknown variable in KEEP=, DROP= or RENAME= of an output data set gives a WARNING and the step completes (an unknown KEEP= variable leaves a data set without variables, an unknown RENAME= pair is ignored). IN= on PROC PRINT DATA= is ERROR 22-7. WHERE= on an output data set is not implemented yet and fails loud.

  • A BY statement inside a DO, IF or SELECT block was ignored; it now fails loud.

  • LEAVE inside a SELECT group leaves the SELECT, not the enclosing DO loop. An iterative DO evaluates its start, TO and BY values before it assigns the start to the index, so do i = 1 to i; uses the value of i before the loop.

  • An assignment to SUBSTR() on the left of = is checked as its own context of SUBSTR; CONSTANT('EXACTINT', 1E300) stops the step with the step exception in a step that runs once and fails loud elsewhere.

  • Dates have no 29 February in years divisible by 4000.

  • Log messages that describe sasonr’s own handling name sasonr as the subject: “NOTE: sasonr stopped processing this step because of errors.”, “NOTE: Due to ERROR(s) above, sasonr set option OBS=0, enabling syntax check mode.” and “NOTE: sasonr went to a new line when INPUT statement reached past the end of a line.”

  • Expressions of the DATA step, WHERE and PROC SQL are parsed with one operator table. sasonr treats the following as described here: IN, NOT IN and IN: bind tighter than the other comparison operators in the DATA step (a <= b in (0, 5) is a <= (b in (0, 5))); in WHERE, -a ** b is (-a) ** b, ** binds tighter than MIN and MAX, and NOT takes a MIN/MAX operand; in PROC SQL, ^ (NOT) takes a comparison as its operand; colon comparisons (=:, <: …) take part in comparison chains; BETWEEN accepts constant numeric bounds in either order; ||, LIKE and CONTAINS in WHERE and PROC SQL take character operands only (a numeric operand is an error); ** with invalid arguments (0 ** 0, a negative base with a fractional exponent) gives a missing value with the invalid-argument NOTE, and with constant operands it is folded at compile time; WHERE conditions are evaluated without data-error NOTEs. These shapes now fail loud: NOT as an operand of `+ - * /in WHERE, a PROC SQL comparison chain that starts with a colon comparison, a chain of three or more links with a colon comparison,BETWEENwith mixed or descending character bounds, a function ERROR or a division by zero in a WHERE condition,%’and%"outside%STR,%NRSTR,%QUOTEand%NRQUOTE`, and the remainders of a statement with a missing semicolon other than the supported ones.

Macro language

  • A numbered ERROR in text a macro generated writes NOTE: Line generated by the invoked macro "NAME". (the innermost macro) and the generated line with its marker; one on a line of an included file writes that line as n +text with its marker. An invalid statement (ERROR 180-322) in a DATA step adds no variables to the data set the stopped step leaves.

  • %INCLUDE 'path'; alone on its line reads the file as if its lines followed the statement, also in a step and nested: they take the next line numbers and are not echoed (NOSOURCE2). A %INCLUDE in a program with macro definitions or open-code %IF/%DO, with a fileref or options, of a missing file, or under OPTIONS SOURCE2 fails loud.

  • OPTIONS MPRINT writes the text each macro call generates, up to each semicolon and after the last one, as MPRINT(NAME): text (NAME: the macro whose body wrote it), with its blanks and line breaks collapsed to one blank and wrapped at LINESIZE. Several blanks or a line break inside a quoted string fail loud.

  • The macro processor interleaves with step execution: a step runs as soon as it is complete, so values created with CALL SYMPUT(X) and PROC SQL INTO: are available to the macro code that follows.

  • Global statements outside a step take effect as soon as they are complete, before the macro code after them runs. OPTIONS LINESIZE=MAX and NONOTES inside PROC DATASETS or PROC SQL apply to the macro code after them; other in-step settings followed by a %SYSFUNC NOTE fail loud. The positive and negative forms of an option in one OPTIONS statement apply in the order written.

  • Text generated by a macro call has the line of the call (NOTE places, ERROR lines and fail-loud messages).

  • Automatic macro variables: SYSLAST and SYSDSN follow _LAST_, SYSFILRC is set by FILENAME, and SYSCC, SYSRC and SYSFILRC can be assigned with %let. Other automatic macro variables fail loud.

  • _LAST_: PROC SQL CREATE VIEW sets it, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE do not, APPEND sets it to BASE=, and a DATA step stopped by an ERROR sets it to its new output data set.

  • %SYSFUNC NOTEs are wrapped at LINESIZE; single quotes inside %LET values hide macro triggers.

PROC SQL

  • OUTOBS=, INOBS= and LOOPS= (also in RESET) take an integer constant: 2.5, -1 or a name give ERROR 22-322 and the rest of the step is not executed. A GROUP BY or ORDER BY column number that is not a positive integer gives “ERROR: GROUP BY clause requires a positive column number.” (ORDER BY alike); ORDER BY -1 no longer leaves the rows unordered.
  • INSERT … SET: a column missing from a SET clause is missing in that row (. or blank), and a value of the wrong type in any SET clause gives “ERROR: It is invalid to assign a numeric expression to a character value using the SET clause.” (and the character-to-numeric message) with no row inserted. A PROC SQL step stopped by an ERROR sets SYSERR to 1012.
  • PROC SQL expressions are evaluated as R calls, without a text round trip.
  • Own recursive-descent SQL parser; DuckDB runs joins and grouping, and SAS semantics are applied in R: missing values, remerging of summary statistics with the remerge NOTE, CALCULATED, INTO :macro-variable and SQLOBS.
  • Computed character columns get fixed lengths (CAT functions of column arguments 200, of constant arguments the length of the value).
  • The NOTE for an out-of-range function argument (Invalid argument to function MDY. Missing values may be generated.) is written; other function data-error NOTEs in PROC SQL fail loud.
  • The summary functions MEAN, CSS, USS, VAR and STD are computed from sequential sums in row order; order-dependent statistics on rows whose order is not fixed fail loud unless the result does not depend on the order.

Procedures

  • PROC MEANS builds its output as ODS tables (the Summary table, with the BY groups, the titles and the column headers); the listing and the HTML destination render the same table. sas_html(x, file, log = FALSE) writes the procedure output of a result as an HTML document (style sheet system.file("css", "sasonr.css", package = "sasonr")). The HTML destination is open when a program starts; ODS HTML CLOSE; and ODS HTML; close and reopen it. ODS HTML FILE= and the other ODS HTML options fail loud.
  • ODS OUTPUT Summary=<data set>; (or Means.Summary=) writes the MEANS Summary table to WORK, with its data set NOTEs. MATCH_ALL, PERSIST=, BY groups and the ODS actions (CLOSE, SELECT, EXCLUDE, …) fail loud.
  • Options that take an integer constant fail with ERROR 22-322 for a fractional value instead of truncating it: PROC MEANS MAXDEC=, FW=, QNTLDEF= / PCTLDEF=; PROC FREQ BINOMIAL LEVEL=, RELRISK COLUMN=. PROC FREQ BINOMIAL(ALPHA=) is an ERROR (ALPHA= is not a BINOMIAL suboption), TABLES ALPHA= and BINOMIAL P= need a number, and PROC FORMAT DEFAULT= needs a number. BINOMIAL P= above 1 is a percentage (P=1.5 tests 0.015). PROC MEANS MAXDEC=-1, an ALPHA= outside (0, 1) and a negative WAYS value give their WARNING and the procedure runs.
  • PROC SORT, PRINT, MEANS / SUMMARY, FREQ, TRANSPOSE, CONTENTS, DATASETS, APPEND, DELETE and FORMAT (VALUE / INVALUE).
  • PROC MEANS / SUMMARY: sums in observation order and the moment statistics (CSS, USS, VAR, STD, STDERR, CV, T, KURTOSIS), computed with and without FREQ and WEIGHT and for the VARDEF= values DF, N, WDF and WEIGHT; T is capped at +-99999.99; STD and CV are reported as 0 when the variance is negligible against the squared mean; a negative CSS is missing. SKEWNESS, PRT and the confidence limits are approximate. MAXDEC= uses the w.d display engine; the printed table chooses its default decimals and splits wide tables into panels.
  • PROC FREQ: tables and OUT=, the chi-square family, FISHER and EXACT FISHER, the 2x2 EXACT CHISQ, BINOMIAL, Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistics (SCORES=TABLE / RANK), the common odds ratio and relative risks, the Breslow-Day test, RISKDIFF and RELRISK (Wald, Agresti-Caffo, Hauck-Anderson, Newcombe and exact unconditional limits), TESTP= / TESTF=, MISSPRINT and BY groups. Requests outside the supported layouts fail loud.

Functions, formats and rounding

  • UPCASE, LOWCASE and PROPCASE map letters outside ASCII with the case mapping of a UTF-8 session (before: they failed loud). They still fail loud in an R session that is not UTF-8, for invalid UTF-8 bytes and for a letter whose other case has a different number of bytes. The PROPCASE page lists which characters start a word.
  • In a UTF-8 session the length of a character variable counts bytes: a value is cut to its first n bytes and padded with blanks to n bytes, and LENGTH, LENGTHN and LENGTHC count bytes. A cut inside a multi-byte character fails loud. New KLENGTH counts characters (0 for a blank argument). Lengths taken from values (literals, R data frames, PROC SQL, PROC TRANSPOSE) count bytes too. Every other function, PUT and INPUT with a character argument that has a byte outside ASCII fail loud (sasonr_strict_error), as do CALL SYMPUT, SYMPUTX and SORTC; an INPUT statement reading such records is not supported.
  • In a UTF-8 session SUBSTR counts positions and lengths in bytes; a start or end inside a multi-byte character fails loud, as do SUBSTR on the left of =, %SYSFUNC(SUBSTR()) and PROC SQL calls with a value that has bytes outside ASCII. New KSUBSTR counts characters; for ASCII values it is SUBSTR, a value with bytes outside ASCII fails loud.
  • ANY* and NOT* take the class of a character outside ASCII from a table of measured classes: every code point from U+00A0 to U+00FF, plus U+0100, U+0152, U+0391, U+4E2D and U+20AC. Among them, the multiplication and division signs are neither letters nor punctuation, the micro sign is a lower case letter, the ordinal indicators and U+4E2D are letters that are neither upper nor lower case, the no-break space is a space and the soft hyphen is not printable. U+1D11E is known to be neither a letter nor punctuation; its other classes and all other characters outside ASCII fail loud. New ANYPRINT and NOTPRINT find the first printable character (blank to tilde in ASCII) or the first character that is not printable.
  • In a UTF-8 session more character functions accept values with bytes outside ASCII and count in bytes: INDEX, INDEXW, INDEXC, FIND, FINDW, FINDC, VERIFY, COUNT, COUNTC, COUNTW, the ANY* and NOT* functions, TRANWRD, TRANSTRN, LEFT, RIGHT, TRIM, STRIP, COMPBL, the CAT functions, SCAN, SUBSTRN, COMPRESS, TRANSLATE, REVERSE and REPEAT. Character lists and delimiters are sets of bytes; the I modifier and the class modifiers recognise ASCII characters only; ANY* and NOT* classify the characters of a table of measured classes (see above) and return the position of the first byte. A result that would leave part of a multi-byte character fails loud. A CAT result cut inside a character by a shorter target variable is blank, with the buffer WARNING and _ERROR_. The colon comparison (=:) truncates in bytes, and $w., $CHARw. and $QUOTEw. count bytes (a cut inside a character fails loud). %SYSFUNC and PROC SQL calls of these functions, $UPCASEw. and the modifiers of SCAN, COUNTW and FINDW (other than E) with such values still fail loud.
  • About 190 SAS functions as sas_f_<name>(), about 100 formats and informats, PUT() / INPUT() and user formats from PROC FORMAT. Missing and invalid arguments write the log NOTEs, set _ERROR_ and give missing results; arguments are converted between numeric and character, and the number of arguments is checked.
  • A direct call of a sas_f_* function from R code is checked as in a DATA step: approximate and unsupported functions follow sasonr.strict (sasonr_strict_error, or with sasonr.strict = FALSE a sasonr_strict_warning once per function and R session), arguments outside the exact input domain follow the same gate, and a data error (an invalid argument, invalid data) gives the documented result with a warning of class sasonr_data_error that carries the NOTE text. sas_f_put() and sas_f_input() take the format or informat as text ("8.2") and check it against the registry.
  • Every sas_f_* function has a reference page with the SAS syntax, parameter descriptions, the differences from base R and examples.
  • ROUND rounds half away from zero with a small relative fuzz and returns the double nearest to the decimal multiple; ROUNDE and ROUNDZ follow their documented definitions. Values at the edge of the fuzz window fail loud.
  • One display engine writes every number that becomes text: w.d, Z, COMMA, DOLLAR, NEGPAREN, PVALUE, PERCENT, the BEST formats, E notation, PROC listings and macro values. Values whose formatted text sasonr cannot determine exactly (some very wide decimals, long integers with decimals, narrow BEST widths, some E forms) fail loud.
  • MOD and MODZ compute exact remainders; YRDIF supports the 30/360, ACT/365 and ACT/360 bases and the AGE and ACT/ACT bases where the result is exact; INTCK and INTNX support the WEEKDAY, TENDAY and SEMIMONTH intervals in their plain form; EXIST() reports WORK and SASHELP members, also in PROC SQL; the $HEX informat writes the INPUT NOTE and sets _ERROR_ for invalid data.
